modules.title: Drug Classes, Names & Pharmacology Basics
modules.desc: Generic/brand naming, drug stems, major therapeutic classes, and how drugs work.

lessons.title: Generic vs Brand Names & Drug Stems
lessons.intro: Every drug has one official generic (nonproprietary) name and one or more brand (trade/proprietary) names. The PTCE heavily tests generic↔brand pairs. Learning suffix "stems" lets you identify a drug's class instantly.
bullets: Generic names are lowercase; brand names are capitalized (e.g., lisinopril vs Zestril).
Common stems: -pril = ACE inhibitor, -sartan = ARB, -olol = beta blocker, -vastatin = HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, -prazole = PPI, -tidine = H2 blocker, -azepam/-azolam = benzodiazepine.
Stem exceptions: nystatin is an antifungal for oral candidiasis, not a statin; aripiprazole is an antipsychotic, not a PPI.
-sartan: losartan (Cozaar), valsartan (Diovan). -vastatin: atorvastatin (Lipitor), simvastatin (Zocor), rosuvastatin (Crestor).

Antibiotic stems: -cillin = penicillins (amoxicillin); ceph- = cephalosporins (cephalexin/Keflex); -thromycin = macrolides (azithromycin/Zithromax, clarithromycin); -floxacin = fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin/Cipro). -mycin is not one class — vancomycin is a glycopeptide.
On the exam, brand names often appear in the question and you must supply the generic class or a clinical fact.
keyPoints: One generic name, many brand names
Learn stems to identify the class

lessons.title: Cardiovascular & Cholesterol Agents
lessons.intro: The largest PTCE medication group. Know the class, brand name, and key safety point for each.
bullets: ACE inhibitors (-pril): lisinopril (Zestril/Prinivil), enalapril — for HTN/HF; classic dry cough (bradykinin) and angioedema risk.
ARBs (-sartan): losartan, valsartan — same indications as ACEIs without the cough; both classes are teratogenic (avoid in pregnancy).
Beta blockers (-olol): metoprolol (Lopressor = IR tartrate; Toprol-XL = ER succinate), atenolol (Tenormin) — lower HR/BP; caution in asthma, do not stop abruptly.
Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine (Norvasc, dihydropyridine → vasodilation, ankle edema); diltiazem/verapamil (non-DHP → also slow heart rate).
Statins (-vastatin): atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin — lower LDL; report unexplained muscle pain (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis); simvastatin interacts with grapefruit (CYP3A4).
Diuretics: hydrochlorothiazide/HCTZ (thiazide, hypokalemia), furosemide/Lasix (loop, "loses potassium"), spironolactone (potassium-sparing).

Clopidogrel (Plavix): thienopyridine P2Y12 platelet inhibitor; tablets contain 75 mg clopidogrel. Indicated to reduce MI and stroke in acute coronary syndrome, and in recent MI, recent stroke, or established peripheral arterial disease.

lessons.title: Antibiotics & Anti-Infectives
lessons.intro: Know the major antibiotic classes, their stems, spectrum, and signature safety points.
bullets: Z-Pak = 6 tabs: 500 mg day 1, then 250 mg × 4.
Ceftaroline covers MRSA plus some gram-negatives.

Penicillins (-cillin): amoxicillin and Augmentin for ear infections and strep; watch for allergy/anaphylaxis. Ask about penicillin, cephalosporin, or other allergens first. Severe cephalosporin reactions are reported after penicillin hypersensitivity. Cephalosporins (ceph-/-cef-): cephalexin (Keflex). Generations 1–5 are not steadily broader gram-negative coverage. Macrolides (-thromycin): azithromycin (Zithromax) and clarithromycin. QT risk.

Fluoroquinolones (-floxacin): ciprofloxacin (Cipro), levofloxacin. Box: tendon rupture, tendinitis, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, myasthenia gravis exacerbation. QT is a separate warning, not the box. Use one only if there is no alternative for acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, uncomplicated cystitis, or acute sinusitis. Age over 60 raises rupture risk. Not first choice in children (arthropathy); anthrax and plague are approved.

Tetracyclines: no doxycycline or tetracycline under age 8 or in pregnancy (permanent tooth stain). They chelate with dairy and antacids. Bactrim: sulfa allergy, hyperkalemia, photosensitivity, SJS, TEN, with fatalities reported. Diflucan: vaginal, oropharyngeal, and esophageal candidiasis, plus cryptococcal meningitis. Zovirax oral: shingles, initial and recurrent genital herpes, chickenpox (varicella). Tamiflu, a neuraminidase inhibitor: flu A and B, acute, uncomplicated, age ≥2 weeks, symptoms ≤48 h; prophylaxis if age ≥1 year. Age ≥13: 75 mg twice daily for 5 days.
keyPoints: FQ box: tendon, nerves, CNS, myasthenia

lessons.title: Endocrine: Diabetes & Thyroid
lessons.intro: Diabetes agents are frequently tested by class and mechanism; thyroid drugs have strict administration rules.
bullets: Metformin (Glucophage): first-line biguanide for T2DM. GI upset; take with food.
Sulfonylureas release insulin; main risk is hypoglycemia: glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide.

Hold metformin for iodinated contrast at or before the dose only if eGFR is 30–60, or the pt has a history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure, or the contrast is intra-arterial. Recheck eGFR at 48 h and restart if stable (lactic acidosis). Empagliflozin (Jardiance, -gliflozin): more urinary glucose, genital infections, DKA. Sitagliptin (Januvia, -gliptin). Pioglitazone (Actos, -glitazone): weight gain, fluid, HF caution.

Ozempic (semaglutide) and Victoza (liraglutide) are injectable GLP-1s (weight loss, GI upset). Box: thyroid C-cell tumors. Semaglutide in rodents; liraglutide in rats and mice. Unknown in humans, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). No personal or family MTC, and no MEN 2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2). Ozempic: subcut weekly, start 0.25 mg, then 0.5 mg after 4 weeks. Missed dose: within 5 days.

Insulin: lispro (Humalog) and aspart (NovoLog) ~15 min; Regular short; NPH intermediate; glargine (Lantus) ~24 h, no peak; degludec (Tresiba) ≥42 h. Levemir is discontinued. Unopened: refrigerate, never freeze. Vial in use 28 days, fridge or room. SoloStar 28 days, room temp only; do not refrigerate. Levothyroxine (Synthroid, T4): empty stomach, 30–60 min before breakfast, 4 h from calcium or iron, same brand.
keyPoints: GLP-1 box: no MTC or MEN 2

lessons.title: CNS, Psychiatric & Pain Agents
lessons.intro: Antidepressants, anxiolytics, sedatives, and analgesics — know class, schedule, and key warnings.
bullets: Flumazenil reverses benzos. Naloxone reverses opioids.
Zolpidem (Ambien) and eszopiclone (Lunesta) are C-IV.

SSRIs have no one suffix: fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro). Onset 2–4 weeks. Serotonin syndrome with an MAOI or triptan. -oxetine is not SSRI-only; duloxetine is an SNRI. Lamictal XR: serious rash, including SJS. About 0.8% (8 per 1,000) at ages 2 to 16 on adjunctive IR lamotrigine for epilepsy; 0.3% (3 per 1,000) adults on adjunctive epilepsy therapy. Rare TEN and rash-related death. Not approved under 13.

Duloxetine (Cymbalta): depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain. Venlafaxine (Effexor XR): MDD, GAD, social anxiety, panic, not neuropathic pain. Benzos C-IV (sedation, dependence): alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), diazepam (Valium). NSAIDs: ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), meloxicam (Mobic), celecoxib (Celebrex); GI bleed and CV risk; take with food. Z-drugs can impair the next day.

APAP max 4 g/day (many recommend 3 g). Overdose: hepatotoxic; antidote N-acetylcysteine. Do not combine APAP products. Norco = hydrocodone/APAP. Oxycodone and Norco are C-II; tramadol is C-IV. No constipation tolerance. Sedation and respiratory depression. Concerta (methylphenidate ER): CNS stimulant for ADHD, ages 6 to 65. Box: abuse and misuse can cause addiction, overdose, and death. Imitrex: 5-HT1B/1D; 25, 50, or 100 mg; acute migraine with or without aura in adults; not prevention. Abilify: schizophrenia. Box: higher death in elderly dementia psychosis; not approved for it.

lessons.title: Respiratory, GI & Miscellaneous
lessons.intro: Respiratory inhalers, GI acid agents, and other high-frequency drugs.
bullets: Prime Ventolin HFA. ProAir RespiClick needs no prime. Both are rescue albuterol (SABA).
Salmeterol (LABA) is never used alone in asthma. Fluticasone (Flovent) is the ICS.

Montelukast (Singulair): leukotriene receptor antagonist for asthma and allergic rhinitis. Box: neuropsychiatric effects. PPIs (-prazole; aripiprazole is not one): omeprazole (Prilosec), pantoprazole (Protonix), esomeprazole (Nexium), 30–60 min before the first meal. Long-term: low B12, fractures. Famotidine (Pepcid) is a weaker H2 blocker (-tidine).

Alendronate (Fosamax), a bisphosphonate: plain water, ≥30 min before food, stay upright (esophagitis). Treatment of osteoporosis, postmenopausal women and men: 10 mg daily or 70 mg weekly. Prevention of osteoporosis, postmenopausal women: 5 mg daily or 35 mg weekly. Allopurinol (Zyloprim) prevents gout; colchicine treats the flare. TEN/SJS in about 5 in 10,000 (0.05%). Stop at the first rash.

Loratadine (Claritin) does not sedate; diphenhydramine (Benadryl) does. Tamsulosin: alpha-1A blocker for signs and symptoms of BPH, not hypertension. Prednisone, a systemic glucocorticoid: tabs 5, 10, or 20 mg; short-term adjunct in rheumatoid arthritis. Tri-Sprintec (norgestimate and ethinyl estradiol) is a combination OC that prevents pregnancy. Box: smoking raises serious CV events. Contraindicated over 35 if the pt smokes.
keyPoints: Treat: 10 mg daily or 70 mg weekly

modules.title: High-Alert, LASA & Special-Population Medications
modules.desc: High-alert drugs, look-alike/sound-alike pairs, monitoring-intensive agents (former dedicated NTI list), and pregnancy/teratogen rules.

lessons.title: High-Alert Medications
lessons.intro: High-alert medications bear a heightened risk of significant harm when used in error. The ISMP list is a PTCE favorite.
bullets: High-alert: insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, KCl, chemotherapy, methotrexate.
Trexall for RA: start 7.5 mg PO once weekly. Daily dosing has caused death.

U-100 = 100 units/mL. Wrong insulin doses are common; use an independent double check. Dilute concentrated KCl before IV use. Undiluted rapid IV push can cause fatal cardiac arrest. Also: standard order sets, Tall Man, RPh profile review before ADC removal.

Bleeding is the main harm. Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist), INR: prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and PE, and of thromboembolic complications with AF and/or valve replacement. Also cuts death, recurrent MI, and events such as stroke after MI. Heparin: aPTT and HIT.

Apixaban (Eliquis), factor Xa: cut stroke and systemic embolism in nonvalvular AF; DVT prophylaxis after hip or knee replacement; treat DVT and PE and cut recurrence. Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), factor Xa: same stroke use; treat DVT; treat PE; cut DVT or PE recurrence; DVT prophylaxis, which may lead to PE, after knee or hip replacement.

lessons.title: Look-Alike Sound-Alike (LASA) & Tall Man Lettering
lessons.intro: LASA pairs cause many dispensing errors. ISMP recommends Tall Man lettering to differentiate them.
bullets: Tall Man lettering capitalizes the DISsimilar letters: predniSONE vs prednisoLONE; hydrALAZINE vs hydrOXYzine; DOBUTamine vs DOPamine; niCARdipine vs NIFEdipine.
Also classic LASA pairs: hydrALAZINE (BP)/hydrOXYzine (antihistamine), clonidine/clonazepam, lamotrigine/lamivudine.

Prevention: segregate look-alike products on shelves, add warning labels to bins, use barcode scanning at verification, and read the full name + indication. The goal is to draw attention to the differing letters, not to change pronunciation.

lessons.title: Narrow Therapeutic Index & Monitoring (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. A dedicated NTI-list knowledge area (old 1.8) was removed from the January 2026 outline. Skip this lesson on the default path. These agents still matter as high-alert / monitoring drugs if you want extra review.
bullets: Digoxin (Lanoxin): cardiac glycoside for HF/AFib — toxicity shows nausea, vomiting, and yellow-green visual halos; check level and potassium.
Warfarin: monitor INR; keep dietary vitamin K intake consistent.
Lithium, phenytoin (Dilantin), theophylline, and carbamazepine are other classic NTI drugs requiring levels.
Hypokalemia (low K+) increases digoxin toxicity risk — diuretics that waste potassium compound this.

lessons.title: Pregnancy, Teratogens & Special Populations
lessons.intro: Certain drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy; technicians must recognize teratogens and handling restrictions.
bullets: Known teratogens (avoid in pregnancy): isotretinoin (Accutane), warfarin, methotrexate, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, tetracyclines, valproate, and finasteride.
Statins are not an absolute avoid: stop them in most pregnant patients and weigh the individual need.
Isotretinoin requires the iPLEDGE REMS program with strict pregnancy-prevention measures.

Finasteride: pregnant women should not handle crushed or broken tablets (skin absorption). Dutasteride (Avodart) is a capsule; pregnant women should not handle the capsules because dutasteride can be absorbed through the skin from leakage.
Pediatric caution: tetracyclines (<8 years, tooth staining), fluoroquinolones (cartilage), aspirin in children with viral illness (Reye's syndrome).
The old letter categories (A/B/C/D/X) were replaced by the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) narrative format, but "Category X = teratogen" still appears on older references/exams.

modules.title: Dosage Forms, Routes, Storage & Interactions
modules.desc: Dosage-form handling rules, routes of administration, storage requirements, and major interactions.

lessons.title: Dosage Forms & Routes
lessons.intro: How a drug is formulated determines how it must be handled and administered — a frequent PTCE topic.
bullets: Sublingual (SL) dissolves under the tongue for rapid absorption and bypasses first-pass metabolism (nitroglycerin). Buccal = between cheek and gum.
Enteric-coated (EC) resists stomach acid and dissolves in the small intestine — do NOT crush (aspirin EC, omeprazole).
Extended-release (ER/XL/SR/CR/LA) releases over time — do NOT crush or chew (risk of dose dumping). Toprol-XL is scored and may be split; do not crush or chew it.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT) dissolve on the tongue; effervescent tablets must be fully dissolved in water first. Suspensions: "shake well before use."
Transdermal patches give steady absorption and bypass first-pass; rotate sites, never cut reservoir patches, fold before disposal (fentanyl patch is high-alert).
Many nasal sprays and metered-dose inhalers such as Ventolin HFA require priming before first use or after prolonged non-use. ProAir RespiClick does not require priming.
keyPoints: Do NOT crush or chew EC or ER; Toprol-XL may be split
Prime Ventolin HFA; do not prime ProAir RespiClick

lessons.title: Storage Requirements
lessons.intro: Proper storage preserves potency and safety; the PTCE tests specific temperature requirements.
bullets: Never freeze insulin. Detemir (Levemir) is discontinued in the US.
NTG SL: original glass, tight cap, room temp, so it keeps potency.

Unopened insulin, many vaccines, and some biologics: 2–8°C (36–46°F). Most refrigerated vaccines must not be frozen; some need frozen or ultra-cold storage. In use: Lantus vial 28 days, fridge or room. SoloStar 28 days at room temp only; do not refrigerate. Tresiba 56 days.

Amox susp: discard unused after 14 days; fridge preferable, not required. Azithromycin oral susp: 5–30°C (41–86°F), use within 10 days. Not every reconstituted antibiotic susp is refrigerated. Room temp 20–25°C (68–77°F) is the default for most tabs and caps. Protect from moisture and light.

Opened multi-dose vial: date the puncture; discard in 28 days unless that label says otherwise. Beyond-use never past the manufacturer expiration. For more than one pt, keep it in a clean prep area, away from treatment. If it enters the treatment area, dedicate it to that one pt. HD areas: authorized staff only, and designated areas must include HD storage.
keyPoints: Opened MDV: 28 days unless label differs

lessons.title: Major Drug Interactions
lessons.intro: Technicians flag potential interactions for the pharmacist. Know the classic high-yield combinations.
bullets: Therapeutic duplication: two or more drugs in one class when the combined daily dose risks harm. Flag it for the RPh.
Warfarin + NSAID or aspirin: more bleeding. Warfarin + Bactrim, metronidazole, or a macrolide: higher INR. Keep vitamin K steady. Avoid a sudden jump in leafy greens.
MAOI + SSRI or another serotonergic drug: serotonin syndrome. Avoid; a washout is required.
Sildenafil (Viagra) + a nitrate (nitroglycerin): severe hypotension. Contraindicated.
Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 and raises simvastatin and many other CYP3A4 substrates.

St. John's wort is a strong CYP3A inducer; the effect varies and depends on the preparation. It may weaken combined OCs such as Tri-Sprintec. Back-up contraception during the inducer and for 28 days after it stops.
Biotin in supplements can skew some labs without being noticed, including a falsely low troponin.
ACE inhibitor + spironolactone or a K+ supplement: hyperkalemia. Calcium, iron, and antacids chelate tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and levothyroxine. Separate by several hours.
keyPoints: St. John's wort: CYP3A inducer; 28-day back-up

modules.title: Error Prevention, Reporting & Continuous Quality Improvement
modules.desc: The medication-use process, error categories, reporting programs, and quality-improvement methods.

lessons.title: The Medication-Use Process & the Five Rights
lessons.intro: Medication safety is built on verifying the "five rights" at every step and understanding where errors occur.
bullets: The five rights: right PATIENT, right DRUG, right DOSE, right ROUTE, right TIME. (Some add right documentation and right indication.)
The medication-use process: prescribing → transcribing/order entry → dispensing → administration → monitoring. Errors can occur at each step.
A technician's role: accurate order entry, correct product selection, barcode scanning, and flagging concerns to the pharmacist.
Verify the patient with two identifiers (full name + date of birth) before filling or dispensing.
keyPoints: Five rights: patient, drug, dose, route, time

lessons.title: Error Types, Near Misses & NCC MERP Categories
lessons.intro: Know error severity, the prescription error types on outline 3.5, and the ISMP abbreviations that cause them.
bullets: Near miss: caught before the pt. Report it.
Outline 3.5: wrong dose, quantity, pt, drug, or route. Wrong time and omission are other types, not those examples.
NCC MERP: A = circumstances with error potential; B = did not reach the pt.
C = reached the pt, no harm. D = reached the pt and needed monitoring to confirm no harm and/or an intervention to preclude harm.
E = temporary harm needing intervention; F = hospitalization; G = permanent harm; H = life-sustaining intervention; I = death.
Prospective DUR: daily dose = strength × qty dispensed ÷ days' supply. Outside the set standard, stop and tell the RPh.

ISMP Do Not Use: units not U; international units not IU; daily or every other day, not QD or QOD; morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate, not MS, MSO4, or MgSO4. Write 0.5 mg, not .5 mg. Write 1 mg, not 1.0 mg.

Also: mL not cc; mcg not µg. Spell right eye, left eye, both eyes, right ear, left ear, both ears (not OD, OS, OU, AD, AS, AU). D/C is not discharge or discontinue. HS/hs swaps half-strength and bedtime. Subcut, not SC, SQ, or sub q. 3 times weekly, not TIW (read as 3 times a day).
keyPoints: Near miss = caught before the pt
No U, IU, QD, QOD, MS, MSO4, or MgSO4

lessons.title: Reporting Programs & Recalls
lessons.intro: Know where and how medication errors and adverse events are reported, and the FDA recall classes.
bullets: FDA MedWatch: voluntary reporting of adverse events, product problems, and medication errors (Form 3500 for professionals, 3500B for consumers).

Product integrity: report a product-quality concern to MedWatch when quality, authenticity, performance, or safety is in doubt (suspect counterfeit, contamination, defective components, poor packaging or product mix-up, questionable stability, labeling concerns).
ISMP MERP (Medication Errors Reporting Program): voluntary, CONFIDENTIAL national error reporting to share prevention strategies.

VAERS (Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, for vaccines): anyone may report. Healthcare providers are required to report an adverse event on the VAERS Table of Reportable Events Following Vaccination that occurs within the specified time, and an adverse event the manufacturer lists as a contraindication to further doses.

Recall classes: Class I = reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II = temporary or medically reversible harm, or a remote probability of serious harm; Class III = adverse health consequences not likely.
When a recall occurs: check lot numbers, quarantine affected stock, and follow the recall instructions for return/disposal.
keyPoints: Class I = serious adverse health consequences or death

lessons.title: Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI)
lessons.intro: Quality improvement uses structured methods to reduce errors and improve processes.
bullets: RCA finds the process failure, not a person to blame.
PDSA is Plan-Do-Study-Act. Med rec: admission, transfer, discharge.

Independent double check: two qualified staff separately verify insulin, anticoagulants, and chemotherapy before dispensing or administration. Acute-care high-alert also: neuromuscular blockers (succinylcholine, rocuronium, vecuronium); oral sulfonylureas (glimepiride, glipiZIDE, glyBURIDE). U-500 and oral methotrexate for nononcologic use are singled out.

Community high-alert also: azaTHIOprine, cycloSPORINE, tacrolimus (oral and parenteral) and pediatric liquids that must be measured. Humulin R U-500 is 500 units/mL, 5 times the insulin in 1 mL of U-100 (100 units/mL). Use only a U-500 syringe. A U-100 syringe can give a 5-times overdose. Do not mix with any other insulin. Do not inject IV.

Prospective DUR, before the Rx is filled or delivered: therapeutic duplication, drug-disease, drug-drug, wrong dose, wrong duration, drug-allergy, abuse or misuse. Retrospective DUR looks at patterns later. Part D concurrent DUR, before each dispense (point of sale or distribution): age or gender, overutilization, underutilization, drug-drug, wrong dose or duration, drug-allergy, abuse or misuse.

modules.title: USP Chapter IDs, Hazardous Drugs & Infection Control
modules.desc: Recognize which USP chapter applies, handle hazardous drugs, and meet 3.6 hygiene and counting-tray cleaning standards. Sterile cleanroom depth and dedicated USP <795> technique are optional/archive — not core 2026 PTCE.

lessons.title: USP Standards Overview
lessons.intro: Know which USP chapter applies. Dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures (old 1.9 / 4.1) were removed from the January 2026 outline — do not treat <795> technique or BUD tables as core tested skills.
bullets: USP <795>: NONSTERILE compounding chapter (oral suspensions, topicals, capsules). Removed as a dedicated 2026 procedure skill — chapter ID only.
USP <797>: STERILE compounding chapter (IV admixtures, injections, ophthalmics). Cleanroom procedure and garbing depth are optional archive, not core PTCE.
USP <800>: safe HANDLING of HAZARDOUS DRUGS across both sterile and nonsterile settings — PPE, containment (C-PEC/C-SEC), and personnel protection.
Beyond-use date (BUD): the date after which a COMPOUNDED preparation must NOT be used — assigned per USP limits and stability data, NOT the manufacturer expiration date.

lessons.title: Sterile Compounding: Cleanroom & Garbing (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Sterile cleanroom design and garbing are CSPT-level skills, not core PTCE content. Do not treat cleanroom categories or risk levels as required exam material.
bullets: Optional enrichment only: ISO 5 = compounding area (PEC/hood), ISO 7 = buffer room, ISO 8 = ante-room. These classes are not a required PTCE category list.
Laminar airflow workbenches provide ISO 5 HEPA-filtered air; work at least 6 inches inside the hood and avoid blocking first air.
If you review garbing, the order is DIRTIEST to CLEANEST: shoe covers → hair/beard cover → face mask → hand hygiene → gown → sterile gloves LAST.
Hand hygiene: scrub hands and forearms before the gown; don sterile powder-free gloves last; sanitize gloves with sterile 70% IPA.
Clean the PEC with sterile 70% isopropyl alcohol; buffer/ante rooms are cleaned per a defined schedule.
keyPoints: Shoes, hair, mask, hands, gown, gloves
Do not memorize cleanroom categories for the PTCE

lessons.title: Hazardous Drugs & Infection Control
lessons.intro: Safe handling protects both patients and workers from hazardous-drug exposure and contamination.
bullets: NIOSH lists hazardous drugs: antineoplastics, hormones, and some antivirals.
HD compounding PPE: two pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves plus an impermeable gown. Add eye, face, and respiratory protection for the risk.
Compound HDs in a C-PEC (BSC or CACI) inside a negative-pressure C-SEC.

Soap and water for at least 20 seconds when hands are visibly soiled, and when caring for pts with suspected or confirmed infection during C. difficile or norovirus outbreaks. If hands are not visibly soiled, an alcohol-based rub is preferred.
CDC don order: gown, then mask or respirator, then goggles or face shield, then gloves over the gown cuff. Doff: gloves, then goggles or face shield, then gown, then mask or respirator.
Outline 3.6: wipe counting trays and counters with 70% isopropyl alcohol between fills. Clean again after penicillin, sulfa, or an HD before the next Rx. Use a dedicated tray for HDs.
Sharps go in a rigid, puncture-resistant, closable container. Never regular trash, recycling, or recapping by hand.
Most vaccines: refrigerate at 2–8°C (36–46°F) and do not freeze. Monitor with a calibrated thermometer and document the temperatures.
keyPoints: 70% IPA between fills; dedicated HD tray

lessons.title: USP <795> nonsterile technique (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures (old 1.9 / related 4.1) were removed. Keep this only as historical review. Default-path study is chapter ID, hazardous-drug handling, and counting-tray/counter hygiene.
bullets: Historical <795> technique topics included BUD assignment by risk, component selection, and nonsterile compounding steps (trituration, geometric dilution, levigation).
Those procedure skills, including nonsterile BUD tables, are not a January 2026 tested knowledge area — do not memorize them on the default path. A BUD/technique item is archive, not core PTCE.
Still in scope nearby: which chapter is <795> vs <797> vs <800>, and 3.6 cleaning of trays, counters, equipment, handwashing, and PPE.

modules.title: Safety Technologies, Workflow & Pharmacist Intervention
modules.desc: Barcode/ADC safeguards, REMS hand-off, pharmacist-intervention triggers (DUR, OTC, substitution), and immunization workflow (VIS before the dose, post-immunization care, VAERS).

lessons.title: Safety Technology & Workflow Safeguards
lessons.intro: Technology and process design reduce dispensing errors at the point of care.
bullets: The tech stops, gathers the facts, and tells the RPh.
Do not override a clinical alert or recommend a product.

Barcode the NDC at verification. An ADC needs RPh profile review before removal. Prospective DUR is at order entry. The tech flags interaction and duplication; the RPh decides. Auxiliary labels: "May cause drowsiness," "Take with food," "Avoid alcohol," "Refrigerate."

REMS examples: iPLEDGE and THALOMID/lenalidomide. TIRF production stopped September 30, 2024; no new enrollments. Clozapine REMS ended June 13, 2025. Tall Man, separate look-alike bins, fewer strengths. FDA pair: buPROPion vs busPIRone. Call the RPh (3.3) for DUR alerts, adverse events, OTC advice, substitution, misuse or adherence, allergies, and interactions.

Overuse: quantity, strength, or duration past the goal, or enough to risk a clinically significant undesirable effect, or both. Underuse: too little to reach the goal, or enough to risk that effect, or both. An adverse event is any untoward medical occurrence with a drug in humans, related or not. A medication error may lack one. Off-label use, misuse, and abuse outside the FDA label are not medication errors.
keyPoints: Do not override a clinical alert

lessons.title: Pharmacist Intervention & Immunization Workflow (VIS / VAERS)
lessons.intro: Outline 3.3 and 3.4 include pharmacist intervention and event reporting. Immunizing pharmacies add VIS (before the dose), post-immunization observation, and VAERS. Purple Book biologics interchangeability is not a 2026 PTCE knowledge area.
bullets: VIS (Vaccine Information Statement): CDC sheet required by federal law before each dose of a covered vaccine. Use the current edition; document the VIS date and the date given. Give it before immunization — not only afterward and not only if the patient asks.
Post-immunization: for most vaccines, observe the patient seated or lying down for 15 minutes (most syncope is within 15 minutes). Some people are observed 30 minutes after a COVID-19 vaccine.
If the patient feels faint, seat them and notify the pharmacist. Do not send them to the parking lot untreated.
VAERS = vaccine adverse events. MedWatch = general FDA drug/device/medication-error reports. Know which system matches the product.
OTC recommendation and therapeutic substitution always go to the pharmacist (3.3).

Purple Book (FDA licensed biologics / interchangeability) is not named on the January 2026 outline — skip it as tested content. Orange Book A/AB remains the small-molecule TE shorthand in Federal notes.
keyPoints: VAERS for vaccines; MedWatch for drugs

modules.title: Reading Prescriptions & SIG Codes
modules.desc: Prescription components, abbreviations, administration supplies, NDC and expiration, and returns.

lessons.title: Parts of a Prescription
lessons.intro: A prescription has defined parts; understanding them is essential for accurate order entry.
bullets: Inscription: the medication name and strength.
Subscription: the dispensing instructions — quantity to dispense and any special preparation.
Signa ("sig"): the directions for the patient (how to take it).
"Disp #30" = dispense a quantity of 30; refills are authorized separately (e.g., "Refills: 2").
Other elements: prescriber info + DEA number (for controls), patient name/DOB/address, date written, and prescriber signature.
Red flags requiring pharmacist clarification: illegible handwriting, unusual dose, missing quantity/sig, dangerous abbreviations.
keyPoints: Subscription = dispensing directions to the pharmacist

lessons.title: Common SIG Codes & Abbreviations
lessons.intro: Recognize the high-frequency abbreviations used in directions. qd and the eye/ear codes are ISMP error-prone: know the meaning, and write the words instead.
bullets: qd means daily, but it is error-prone — do not use it; write daily.
BID (twice daily), TID (three times daily), QID (four times daily).
q4h (every 4 hours), q6h (every 6 hours), qhs (every night at bedtime), PRN (as needed).
Meals/timing: ac (before meals), pc (after meals), hs (at bedtime).
Routes: PO (by mouth), SL (sublingual), PR (rectally), top (topically), IM/IV/SubQ (injections).
Eyes — recognize, do not use: OU = both eyes, OD = right eye, OS = left eye. Write both eyes, right eye, or left eye.
Ears — recognize, do not use: AU = both ears, AD = right ear, AS = left ear. Write both ears, right ear, or left ear.
Amounts: i = one, ii = two, ss = one-half; tab = tablet, cap = capsule, gtt(s) = drop(s), supp = suppository.
Other: ud / ut dict = as directed, STAT = immediately, NR = no refills, DAW = dispense as written.
keyPoints: qhs = at bedtime; qh = every hour
OU/OD/OS and AU/AD/AS: recognize; write the eye or ear

lessons.title: Administration Supplies
lessons.intro: Match the measuring device, diluent, and vaccine needle to the product label.
bullets: Dilaudid oral solution: measure in mL with a graduated oral syringe or cup, not a household teaspoon or tablespoon.
Humulin N label: doses are in units. U-100 = 100 units/mL (the label equates 1 mL with 1 cc). The syringe must be marked for U-100.
FLOVENT HFA: a valved holding chamber (a spacer) and a face mask may be used for young pts. PROAIR RESPICLICK: do not use a spacer or volume holding chamber.
Nebulizer (Class II): sprays a liquid as an aerosol into gas the pt breathes. Includes heated, ultrasonic, gas, venturi, and refillable nebulizers.
Sterile Water for Injection is a parenteral diluent. Do not inject it until it is made approximately isotonic. Not for direct infusion.
Bacteriostatic Water for Injection: 0.9% (9 mg/mL) or 1.1% (11 mg/mL) benzyl alcohol. Neonates: preservative-free Sterile Water for Injection only.
Humalog U-100 label diluent: 0.9% sodium chloride, diluted to 0.1–1 unit/mL.
Adult IM vaccine (CDC): 1 mL or 3 mL syringe, 22- to 25-gauge, 1- to 1.5-inch needle, at 90°. Subcut vaccine: 23- to 25-gauge, 5/8 inch (16 mm), at 45°.
keyPoints: Oral liquid: mL, not a household spoon
U-100 syringe; spacer only if the inhaler allows it

lessons.title: NDC, Lot, and Expiration
lessons.intro: The package carries an NDC, a lot number, and an expiration date.
bullets: 10-digit NDC: labeler (FDA-assigned) – product (strength, form, formulation) – package (size and type). Formats: 4-4-2, 5-3-2, or 5-4-1.
On March 7, 2033, FDA NDCs become 12-digit 6-4-2 by adding leading zeros. HIPAA 11-digit 5-4-2 for reimbursement does not change.
FDA does not intend to object to 10-digit NDCs on labels from March 7, 2033 through March 6, 2036.
Lot number: the package's full manufacturing history. A wrong lot number may misbrand the article.
Past expiration, safety and effect are not guaranteed. Do not use it. Dating follows labeled storage. A product reconstituted at dispensing lists dates for both forms.
The date is on the immediate container and the outer package, unless readable through the outer package. A single-dose container in its carton may show the date on the carton only.

lessons.title: Returns
lessons.intro: Credit returns, non-creditable hazardous waste, and reverse distribution are different paths.
bullets: Credit return: a potentially creditable hazardous waste pharmaceutical is a prescription hazardous waste pharmaceutical expected to receive manufacturer credit, in the original manufacturer packaging (except a recall), undispensed, and unexpired or less than one year past expiration. A reverse distributor receives it to verify that credit.

Non-creditable hazardous waste pharmaceutical: no reasonable expectation of manufacturer credit. Includes investigational drugs, free samples, residues in empty containers, and spill-cleanup material.

Reverse distribute (controlled substances): a DEA-registered reverse distributor acquires them from another registrant or law enforcement to return them to the registered manufacturer, or to a registrant the manufacturer authorizes, or for destruction.
A reverse distributor destroys a controlled substance received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

Returned drug product is identified and held. If storage, shipping, or the container casts doubt on safety, identity, strength, quality, or purity, it is destroyed unless testing proves those standards. Records include lot number, reason, quantity, and disposition.
keyPoints: Credit return: original pack, undispensed, unexpired or <1 year past expiration

modules.title: Pharmacy Calculations
modules.desc: Conversions, days supply, ratio/percent strength, dilution, and IV flow rates. Alligation is not a 2026 tested skill.

lessons.title: Conversions & Household Measures
lessons.intro: Master the unit conversions that underpin most calculation questions.
bullets: Weight: 1 kg = 2.2 lb. Convert lb → kg by dividing by 2.2 (154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg). Metric: 1 g = 1,000 mg; 1 mg = 1,000 mcg.
Volume: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 15 mL = 3 tsp; 1 fl oz ≈ 30 mL; 1 L = 1,000 mL.
Apothecary: 1 grain (gr) ≈ 65 mg (often rounded to 60 mg).

lessons.title: Dosage, Days Supply & Quantity
lessons.intro: The most common calculation tasks: dose size, days supply, and quantity to dispense.
bullets: Dose from strength: (desired dose ÷ available strength) × quantity per unit. 250 mg needed, 125 mg tabs → 2 tabs.
Proportion: a/b = c/d, so a × d = b × c. 250 mg/5 mL = x/20 mL → x = (250 × 20) ÷ 5 = 1,000 mg.
Weight-based dose: mg/kg/day × weight in kg (15 mg/kg/day × 18 kg = 270 mg/day).
Days supply (tablets): quantity ÷ tablets per day. 90 tabs at TID (3/day) = 30 days. Round DOWN for billing.
Insulin days supply: (mL × 100 units for U-100) ÷ units per day. A 10 mL vial = 1,000 units; at 20 units/day lasts 50 days.
Eye/ear drops: total drops = mL × 20 drops/mL; days = total drops ÷ drops per day. 30 mL at 4 drops/day = 150 days.
Inhalers: days = total actuations ÷ puffs per day. 200 actuations at 2 puffs BID (4/day) = 50 days.

lessons.title: Ratio/Percent Strength & Dilution
lessons.intro: Concentration expressions and dilution still appear on the PTCE (outline 4.1). Alligation was removed from the January 2026 calculation list — it lives in the optional archive lesson that follows.
bullets: Percent w/v (solutions) = grams per 100 mL. 0.9% NaCl = 0.9 g per 100 mL; in 500 mL that is 4.5 g. D5W = 5 g dextrose per 100 mL (50 g per 1,000 mL).
Percent v/v = mL per 100 mL. Isopropyl alcohol 70% v/v = 70 mL per 100 mL; in 250 mL that is 175 mL.
Ratio strength: 1:1000 = 1 g per 1,000 mL = 1 mg/mL (epinephrine).
Percent ↔ decimal: divide by 100 (0.75% = 0.0075). Percent w/w (creams) = grams per 100 g. 1% hydrocortisone cream = 10 mg/g, so 0.25% cream = 2.5 mg/g (% × 10).
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2 keeps the amount of drug constant when changing concentration/volume — this remains in scope.
keyPoints: w/v = g/100 mL; w/w = g/100 g

lessons.title: IV Flow Rates
lessons.intro: Flow-rate calculations determine how fast an IV runs.
bullets: mL per hour = total volume ÷ total hours. 1,000 mL over 8 hours = 125 mL/hr.
Drops per minute: gtt/min = (volume in mL ÷ time in minutes) × drop factor (gtt/mL).
Example: 1,000 mL over 6 hours with a 15 gtt/mL set → (1,000 ÷ 360) × 15 ≈ 42 gtt/min.
Know common drop factors: 10, 15, 20 gtt/mL (macro) and 60 gtt/mL (micro).

lessons.title: Alligation (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Alligation was removed from the January 2026 calculation list. Skip it on the default path. Use C1V1 = C2V2 for dilution and concentration.
bullets: Historical method: parts of the higher strength = target − lower; parts of the lower strength = higher − target.
Example (archive only): mix 70% and 20% to make 50% → 30 parts of 70% and 20 parts of 20% = 3:2.
Default 2026 skill: C1V1 = C2V2, percent w/v (g/100 mL) and w/w (g/100 g), and ratio strength (1:1000 = 1 mg/mL).
q136 in the bank is tagged featured:false so it does not enter default exams or weak-area weighting.

modules.title: Insurance Billing & Order Processing
modules.desc: Third-party billing, DAW codes, prior authorization, and coordination of benefits. Not a 2026 PTCE knowledge area — optional archive. The corrected facts stay here for review.

lessons.title: Third-Party Billing & DAW Codes (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. DAW codes and third-party billing are recommended practice, not a PTCE knowledge area. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: DAW codes: DAW 0 = no product selection indicated (default); DAW 1 = substitution not allowed by prescriber; DAW 2 = substitution allowed, patient requested the brand.
Common rejections: "Refill too soon," "NDC not covered," "Prior authorization required," and incorrect days supply or patient DOB.
Patient identity: full name + date of birth are required to match the correct profile; a DOB mismatch is a common rejection cause.
BIN, PCN, Group, and Member ID numbers on the insurance card route the claim to the correct payer.
keyPoints: DAW 0 = no product selection; DAW 1 = prescriber blocks substitution

lessons.title: Prior Authorization & Coordination of Benefits (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Prior authorization and coordination of benefits are recommended practice, not a PTCE knowledge area. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: Prior authorization (PA): the prescriber must justify medical necessity to the insurer BEFORE the claim will pay.
Coordination of benefits (COB) determines which plan is primary when a patient has multiple insurers.
Birthday rule (dependent children on both parents' plans): the primary plan is the parent whose birth MONTH/DAY falls earlier in the calendar year.
For a patient 65 or older covered through current employment (the patient's or a spouse's), the group health plan is primary and Medicare is secondary when the employer has 20 or more employees.
Medicare is primary if that employer has fewer than 20 employees, or if there is no current-employment group plan. Medicaid is generally the payer of last resort.

A cash discount card lowers the cash price and is not billed with insurance on that fill. A manufacturer copay coupon is used with commercial insurance to reduce the copay, and must not be used for Medicare or Medicaid.
keyPoints: PA = prescriber justifies to payer first
Age 65, employer 20+: group plan primary, Medicare secondary
Cash discount is not insurance; copay coupon is commercial only

modules.title: Controlled Substances & DEA Regulations
modules.desc: CSA schedules, DEA forms, refill and transfer rules, recordkeeping, and the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act.

lessons.title: Controlled Substance Schedules
lessons.intro: The Controlled Substances Act (1970) created five schedules based on abuse potential and accepted medical use.
bullets: Schedule I: HIGH abuse potential, NO accepted medical use — heroin and LSD. No prescriptions.

Marijuana split (current as of April 28, 2026): FDA-approved marijuana products and marijuana under a qualifying state medical-marijuana license are Schedule III. Other marijuana stays Schedule I while broader rescheduling is still pending. Older materials that list all marijuana as C-I are out of date.
Schedule II: high abuse potential WITH accepted medical use — oxycodone, hydrocodone/APAP (Norco), morphine, fentanyl, amphetamine (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin).
Schedule III: moderate abuse potential — Tylenol #3 (codeine/APAP), buprenorphine products, anabolic steroids.
Schedule IV: lower abuse potential — benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam), zolpidem (Ambien), tramadol.
Schedule V: lowest abuse potential — some cough preparations with limited codeine (e.g., guaifenesin/codeine), pregabalin (Lyrica).
The DATA 2000 X-waiver was eliminated in December 2022 (MAT Act) — a separate X number is no longer required to prescribe buprenorphine for OUD.
keyPoints: FDA-approved and state-licensed medical marijuana = C-III
C-II examples include opioids and stimulants

lessons.title: Schedule II–V Prescription & Refill Rules
lessons.intro: Refill, transfer, and transmission rules differ by schedule.
bullets: C-II: no refills. Written or EPCS. Phone only for a true emergency.
C-III/IV: 5 refills in 6 months. C-V: no federal cap; stricter state rule.

Multiple C-II Rxs may total 90 days. If the first fills now, each later Rx shows the earliest fill date. Date and sign it that day: pt full name and address; drug, strength, dosage form, qty, directions; prescriber name, address, DEA number. A C-II fax is the original only for an LTCF C-II, a hospice C-II narcotic with hospice noted, or a C-II narcotic compounded for direct parenteral, IV, IM, subcut, or intraspinal infusion. Emergency oral C-II: write it at once, emergency qty only. Follow-up within 7 days, in person or postmarked. Paper face: "Authorization for Emergency Dispensing" and the oral date; attach it to the oral order. On an e-Rx, note the authorization and oral date. If never delivered, notify the nearest DEA office.

CARA partial: rest within 30 days of the written date. Emergency oral rest: 72 h after issue. Cannot supply the full qty: rest within 72 h of the first partial, else notify the prescriber; no more without a new Rx. LTCF or terminal: 60 days. Then the rest is void. Do not exceed the written qty (90 written, 30 then 20, 40 left). Document each partial. C-III–V transfer once, or until refills are gone on a shared real-time database. Unfilled e-Rx C-II–V: once, RPh to RPh, at the pt request, stays electronic; C-III–V refills go with it. Paper C-II cannot. Non-controlled refills follow state law; no federal one-time cap.

lessons.title: DEA Forms, Registration & Recordkeeping
lessons.intro: Specific DEA forms document ordering, theft/loss, destruction, and registration of controlled substances.
bullets: Form 41 destroys pharmacy-owned CS. Form 222 does not.
Form 224 is the pharmacy registration, renewed every 3 years.

Form 222 is single-sheet paper, not the old triplicate, or CSOS. It orders or transfers C-I and C-II. The registrant, or a person named in a power of attorney, signs it. The registrant (or a partner or officer) and the attorney-in-fact both sign the power; two witnesses; keep it with the orders. On a C-II receipt, write the date and quantity on the pharmacy copy of 222 or the CSOS record.

Form 106: theft or significant loss. Written notice to the local DEA office within 1 business day, then electronic Form 106 within 45 calendar days. Paper Form 106 is not accepted. C-II–IV label: "Caution: Federal law prohibits the transfer of this drug to any person other than the patient for whom it was prescribed." C-V does not.

Keep Rxs, inventories, 222s, and invoices at least 2 years. Inventory is biennial. Opened C-II: exact count. Opened C-III–V: estimate unless the container holds more than 1,000 tabs or caps. Reverse distributor: C-II on 222 or CSOS; C-III–V on an invoice. Pt leftovers are take-back (collector, mail-back, or National Take Back Day), never restocked. DEA number: 2 letters + 7 digits; 2nd letter is usually the last-name initial. Check: (1+3+5) + 2×(2+4+6); last digit of the sum is the 7th. Store C-II locked in a substantial cabinet, or dispersed among non-controls so they are not obvious.

lessons.title: Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (CMEA)
lessons.intro: CMEA restricts OTC sales of pseudoephedrine and ephedrine to curb methamphetamine production.
bullets: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) and ephedrine are kept behind the counter (not a prescription, but restricted). Products must be stored behind the counter or in a locked cabinet.
Daily sales limit: 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base, ephedrine base, or phenylpropanolamine base per purchaser per day.
30-day purchase cap: 9 grams of the base per purchaser, of which not more than 7.5 grams of the base may be mail-order.
Requirements: photo ID and a written or electronic logbook (purchaser name, address, and signature; date and time; product; quantity), except one sales package of not more than 60 mg pseudoephedrine.

Base, not the salt. A 30 mg pseudoephedrine HCl tablet contains 24.6 mg of pseudoephedrine base. 146 of those tablets are 3.5916 g of base, under the 3.6 g daily limit. 366 of those tablets equal the 9.0 g 30-day purchase limit.
keyPoints: 3.6 g base/day; 9 g base/30 days (≤7.5 g mail-order)
Photo ID + logbook (name, address, signature); 60 mg PSE package exception

lessons.title: Restricted Programs: REMS, iPLEDGE & CMEA (2.4)
lessons.intro: Knowledge area 2.4 is federal restricted-drug processing: pseudoephedrine (CMEA) and the REMS programs that are still in effect. A technician stops on a REMS reject and notifies the pharmacist.
bullets: On a REMS reject: stop, do not override, tell the RPh.
A paper waiver does not replace a REMS authorization.

REMS adds FDA steps for a known serious risk: certification, enrollment, labs, or a Medication Guide with each fill. Clozapine REMS ended June 13, 2025. Do not enroll or confirm an ANC in a REMS. Neutropenia risk, the box, and the Medication Guide remain. The prescriber monitors ANC, per the labeling.

iPLEDGE (isotretinoin, a teratogen): prescriber, certified pharmacy, and every pt enroll, whether or not they can get pregnant. Max 30-day supply, no refills, authorize each dispense. Pts who can get pregnant: 7 days from pregnancy-test collection. The 19-day lockout is not current. If missed, repeat the test now.

TIRF production stopped September 30, 2024. No new pt, prescriber, or pharmacy enrollments. Leftover supply only for already-enrolled pts, while applications stay approved. It was transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl for opioid-tolerant pts. THALOMID (thalidomide) and REVLIMID (lenalidomide) are current pregnancy-prevention REMS. CMEA: 3.6 g base/day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g base/30 days, of which ≤7.5 g base may be mail-order. Photo ID, logbook, behind the counter.

modules.title: Patient Privacy, Counseling & Consumer Protection Laws
modules.desc: HIPAA, OBRA-90, and the consumer-protection statutes that shape pharmacy practice.

lessons.title: HIPAA & Patient Privacy (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. HIPAA protects patients' health information and gives them specific rights. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: HIPAA safeguards Protected Health Information (PHI) — any individually identifiable health information.
Pharmacies must provide a Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP) explaining how PHI is used and disclosed.
Minimum necessary applies to most uses and disclosures. It does not apply to a disclosure to, or a request by, a health care provider for treatment.
PHI may be shared without authorization for Treatment, Payment, and healthcare Operations (TPO).
Avoid discussing patient information in public areas. Verify identity before releasing information. Shred PHI documents.

lessons.title: OBRA-90 & Counseling Requirements (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990 established counseling and DUR requirements. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: OBRA-90 mandates a prospective drug utilization review (DUR) before dispensing Medicaid prescriptions.

For each Medicaid beneficiary or caregiver who presents a prescription, the pharmacist offers to counsel on matters the pharmacist judges significant. The offer is not limited to new prescriptions. The patient may decline. Where state law is broader, follow the stricter rule.
Counseling content: drug name, purpose, how to take, side effects, storage, and what to do about a missed dose.
Technicians facilitate counseling offers but the pharmacist provides the clinical counseling.
keyPoints: OBRA-90 = Medicaid DUR + offer to counsel (not only new Rx)

lessons.title: Consumer Protection & Packaging Laws
lessons.intro: Several federal laws govern drug safety, labeling, and packaging.
bullets: Pure Food and Drug Act (1906): banned adulterated and misbranded drugs. The start of federal drug regulation.
FDCA (1938), after the sulfanilamide elixir disaster: drugs must be proven safe. It created the FDA's modern authority.
Durham-Humphrey (1951): Rx (legend) vs OTC. Kefauver-Harris (1962): proven safe and effective, and it established GMP.
PPPA (1970): child-resistant containers for most Rxs and many OTC drugs. The CPSC enforces it, not the FDA. SL nitroglycerin is exempt.
A prescriber may request non-child-resistant packaging for one Rx only. Only the pt may make a blanket request for all of that pt's Rxs. Document the request.
ADA packaging: easy-off caps, large-print labels, talking labels, and Braille labels.
When FDA requires a Medication Guide, give it with every fill, including refills, not only the first fill. Some REMS programs include this step.
Drug Listing Act: every drug has an NDC that identifies the labeler, the product, and the package size.
keyPoints: 1938 safe; 1951 Rx vs OTC; 1962 effective + GMP
Only the pt may blanket-request non-CRC

modules.title: Agencies, Recalls & Practice Regulations
modules.desc: Regulatory agencies, FDA medication recalls (2.5), hazardous and non-hazardous pharmaceutical waste (2.1), DSCSA product tracing (2.6), and workplace practice rules.

lessons.title: Regulatory Agencies & Their Roles (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Know which agency does what — a common exam distinction. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: FDA: drug safety, approval, labeling, recalls, MedWatch, and REMS programs.
DEA: enforces the Controlled Substances Act; registration, schedules, and diversion control.
State Boards of Pharmacy: license pharmacists/technicians and regulate practice within the state.
OSHA: workplace safety — hazardous chemicals, bloodborne pathogens, Safety Data Sheets (SDS).
CDC: immunization guidance and public-health recommendations (with ACIP for vaccines).
NIOSH: identifies hazardous drugs and safe-handling guidance.

lessons.title: Recalls, Expiration & Stock Management
lessons.intro: Outline 2.5 is FDA requirements for medication recalls. Handling recalled and expired stock protects patients. Take-back is a separate 2.3 workflow for patient-owned leftovers.
bullets: Class I: reasonable probability of serious harm or death. Class II: temporary or medically reversible harm, or a remote probability of serious harm. Class III: adverse consequences unlikely.
Depth = wholesale, retail, or consumer. A Class I medication recall usually reaches the consumer, and pts who received that lot are notified.
The firm initiates a recall; FDA may request one. Pull the matching lots, quarantine, document, and follow the return instructions.
FEFO (first-expired, first-out). Never dispense expired drug. Pull expired or damaged units from active stock.
The NDC (labeler–product–package) identifies the recalled product and the return.
A market withdrawal is not a recall: the firm pulls product for a minor violation that would not usually trigger legal recall action.
A stock recovery is not a recall: product that was not marketed, or never left the firm's direct control, and no part of the lot was released for sale or use.
A lot-specific recall is not a pt take-back of leftover home meds.
keyPoints: I serious or death; II reversible; III unlikely

lessons.title: Technician Scope of Practice & Workplace Safety (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Technicians work under pharmacist supervision within defined legal boundaries. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: Technicians may: enter orders, fill/count medications, manage inventory, process insurance, and compound under supervision.
Technicians may NOT: provide clinical counseling, perform the final DUR/clinical verification, or take new verbal prescriptions (varies by state).
The pharmacist is responsible for the final check and all clinical decisions.
When a federal rule and a state rule differ, follow the stricter requirement.
Safety Data Sheets (SDS) describe chemical hazards; OSHA requires they be accessible to staff.
State laws and Boards of Pharmacy set technician registration/licensure and ratio requirements.
keyPoints: Stricter of federal or state law applies

lessons.title: DSCSA Essentials for Technicians
lessons.intro: DSCSA (knowledge area 2.6, added on the January 6, 2026 outline) is the federal track-and-trace law for prescription drugs. Learn durable duties — serialization, authorized partners, suspect vs illegitimate handling, and 6-year records — not rapidly changing exemption end-dates.
bullets: Product identifier: a unique serialized ID, usually a 2D data matrix, with NDC, serial number, lot number, and expiration date.

Current electronic exchange is Transaction Information (product, lot, dates, and the parties) plus a Transaction Statement (the seller attests it is authorized and did not knowingly ship suspect or illegitimate product).
Transaction History was retired in November 2023. Do not memorize TI + TH + TS as the current required set.
Authorized trading partners only: licensed or registered manufacturers, wholesale distributors, dispensers (pharmacies), and repackagers.

Suspect product: reason to believe it may be counterfeit, diverted, stolen, intentionally adulterated, or unfit. Do not dispense. Quarantine it, notify the RPh, and verify the identifier (NDC, serial, lot, and expiration).

Illegitimate product: credible evidence of those same defects. Within 24 hours of that determination, notify FDA (Form FDA 3911) and immediate trading partners. Keep DSCSA transaction records for 6 years, not the 2-year CSA clock.
FDA used phased milestones for electronic package-level tracing. The exam focus is these tech duties, not a specific exemption end date.
keyPoints: TI + TS current; TH retired Nov 2023
Illegitimate: FDA 3911 within 24 hours; records 6 years

lessons.title: Hazardous & Non-Hazardous Pharmaceutical Waste (2.1)
lessons.intro: Knowledge area 2.1 is federal storage, handling, and disposal of non-hazardous and hazardous pharmaceutical waste, including EPA P-list waste, plus the OSHA exposure steps tested with it.
bullets: Do not flush hazardous-waste drugs. EPA banned that sewer path in 2019.
U-list is toxic, not acute: cyclophosphamide U058, lindane U129.

P-list is acute when that chemical is the sole active ingredient. Warfarin above 0.3% is P001. Nicotine is P075, except FDA-approved OTC nicotine replacement, which was removed. Ignitable, corrosive, reactive, or toxic waste can still be hazardous off the lists. Other drug waste is non-hazardous. Not on the P-list does not mean trash or the drain.

Lists cover unused commercial products (pure, technical grade, or sole active), off-specification product, container residue, and spill residue. Residue is hazardous unless the container is empty: a stock bottle, dispensing bottle, vial, or ampule up to 1 liter or 10,000 pills, or a unit-dose, once emptied the usual way. A scheduled hazardous-waste drug is not sewered. Collect, store, transport, and dispose of it under DEA rules. Destroy it by a method DEA has publicly deemed non-retrievable, or combust it at a permitted facility named in the EPA rule.

Colors often used: black RCRA, yellow trace chemo, red biohazard including sharps, blue or white non-hazardous. Follow the vendor if labels differ. Federal duty is segregation, not one color code. No hand recap. Sharps: rigid, puncture-resistant, closable. After a stick: wash, report, PEP. Eyewash 15 minutes, then the SDS. Know the spill kit. Staff must be able to reach the SDS (Hazard Communication).
